subsection.name: Writing the view
subsection.p:
Scope Views extend the Scope base class org.scopemvc.view.swing.SPanel in order to bind Scope SComponents to data in the model class.
There is no event handling in Scope Views. Scope view components issue controls which are intercepted by controllers and executed in models.
For more information about Scope views, see Using SPanel.

In your SPanel, you can put either standard Swing components or Scope's SComponents. It's also possible to add a JPanel containing other components, including Scope's SComponents.
When the SPanel is bound to a Controller and a Model object, it browses automatically all the components it contains at any level of nesting, and bind that component if it's a SComponent to the appropriate property in the bound model.

subsection.name: Synchronizing the view with the model
subsection.p: The synchronization is done automatically if the model extends BasicModel and fires the appropriate ModelChangeEvents, otherwise you have to explicitely call refresh() on the SPanel.

subsection.name: When to use a Scope component or a Swing component
subsection.p:
When you are building a GUI screen, you need to choose for each component if it’s a Scope SComponent, or a standard Swing component.
The following flowchart gives some guidelines about when to use or not to use SComponents.
Additional rules are:
Don’t use SPanels if you don’t have to bind them with a model independent of the parent; use JPanel instead.
If there is not yet a Scope version for a Swing component, use the Swing version and do the model binding manually or wait for a Scope version...

subsection.name: Complex event handling
subsection.p:
Scope provides by default an event handling for most common GUI events, like ActionPerformedEvent on buttons, ListSelectionChangeEvent on lists. Those events are caught by Scope and forwarded to the controller as controls.
Those controls are then handled by the Controller in the doSomething() methods. Those methods should contain only business logic or presentation logic calling some business logic.

In some cases, there are some events fired by the Swing components that are not handled by Scope. In that case, you need first to determine if the event will use only the view or if it will interact with the model and the application logic.
For the first case, you can implement the event listener as in a normal Swing application.
In the second case, the recommanded solution is to write in your SPanel subclass a listener to that event, then create a Control with an ID unique to that event and optionally containing the parameters from that event, then issue the control to the controller with the issueControl() method.
